The surrender of the Earl of Cornwallis at Yorktown closed the career in America of the only British general who had shown commanding gifts in the field.

It closed also the revolution itself.

The southern campaign had been undertaken at the wish and upon the plan of Cornwallis.

He knew how pronounced division of opinion was in the South, and how certain a hold could be gotten there upon the sympathy of scores of men who could be of the utmost service to an army in the field.

He knew how important it was to close the southern ports, and particularly the Chesapeake, in order to shut out the supplies that came steadily in from over the sea.

He believed that an effectual blow struck from the South at Virginia, after the reduction of the far southern ports, would secure for the British an almost commanding position on the continent.

Had Clinton helped him promptly, instead of grudging him aid; had he been enabled to move rapidly and in force as he had planned, he might have accomplished his purpose effectually, even brilliantly.

Even as it was, there had been something very striking about the manner in which he had fought his way from the far southern coasts to Yorktown; the boldness with which he had dared to risk all his connections to deliver a blow; the success with which he had beat off the Americans whenever he was himself in personal command; the comparative freedom with which he had moved in Virginia, despite the gathering strenth of the forces under Lafayette.

It was the express orders of Clinton, his superior, that he had caged him at Yorktown; and it was but seven thousand men he yielded to his fourteen thousand besiegers and de Grasse's fleet in the bay.

It was characteristic of Sir Henry Clinton that he did not start from New York to bring the long-needed aid until the very day of his comrade's surrender.

MISSISSIPPI NEWS
NEGROES SPIRITED AWAY.
Meridian, Miss., Aug. 18.—Two negroes arrested on suspicion of having held up and made insulting remarks to Mrs. Curtis Robertson Sunday afternoon were spirited away by the sheriff last night shortly after dark, when he placed them under heavy guard in an automobile and sent them to another county. Where they were last night he would not say.

It was quietly made known this afternoon, according to officers that a lynching was feared, but if there was any demonstration it did not become generally known.

Mrs. Robertson was returning from Causeyville to the city Sunday afternoon when two armed negroes stepped into the road and commanded her to stop. Mrs. Robertson pulled a revolver from under the cushion of her buggy and fired. The shot went wild, but the negroes fled. Her horse became frightened, and though she fired three times more she did not hit a negro.

Two negroes were arrested shortly afterward in the vicinity of the hold-up. They are Willie Kersey, aged 16, up. They are Willie Kersey, aged 16, and Ben Boney, aged 23. Whether Mrs. Robertson identified them of ficers would not say.

CYCLONIC STORM NEAR KOSCIUSKO McADAMS SUFFERS DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY BUT NO LIVES ARE LOST WRONG MEN NEAR LYNCHED Two Negroes Arrested for Attempted Criminal Assault Found to Be the Wrong Parties After Having Been Spirited Away.
Kosciusko.—A cyclone struck McAdams, a small station seven miles west of this place, on the afternoon of Aug. 20, destroying the railroad station house, a seed house, the residence of Mrs. Francis Gowan and the mill shed of Gowan Bros., and doing other damage.

A negro cabin on Mr. Gowan's farm, where five negroes were housed, was blown to pieces and the negroes left sitting in the rain, unhurt.

No one was hurt in Mr. Gowan's house except his little daughter, who sustained a bruised shoulder by the piano being blown against her.

The twister was only about 60 yards wide and soon spent its force.

Nearly Lynched Wrong Men.

Meridian.—A case of mistaken identity that threatened a lynching developed here Aug. 20, when James Whitehead and Norman Elliott, two negroes, were arrested and placed in the county jail on a charge of attempting to assault Mrs. Curtis Robertson, wife of a well known citizen, as she was returning in a buggy with her baby from a visit to Causeyville on Aug. 15.

Two other negroes, Willie Kirksey and Ben Boney, were arrested after being identified by Mrs. Robertson, and were placed in the county jail. They were spirited to Jackson on the night of Aug. 16 to prevent the threatened mob's violence.

The grand jury of Aug. 20 indicted Kirksey and Boney and it was found soon after that they were innocent and that Whitehead and Elliott were the guilty negroes, both confessing, but saying that they only asked the lady to let them ride and that they ad no evil intention.

The new jail will be constructed on the city stable site, Fifth street and Twenty-sixth avenue. The plans call for a thoroughly sanitary building, equipped with every modern jail convenience.

Allen Westbrooks must pay the death penalty for the murder of his mother-in-law, Mrs. C. C. Cleveland. Such was the verdict of the jury in the Amite county circuit court at Liberty. The jury members who condemned Westbrooks reached their conclusion on Aug. 17 in less than thirty minutes after they took the case. Westbrooks was twice indicted by the grand jury, once for the murder of C. C. Cleveland and the other for the murder of Mrs. Cleveland. On trial Westbrooks attempted to set up a defense of emotional insanity. The crime for which Westbrooks was convicted was one of the bloodiest ever committed in Amite county. On the morning of June 28 it was proven Westbrooks went to the Cleveland home, and there shot down his father-in-law in cold blood.

MURDERER TO PEN
Slayer of Wellston Farmer Hurried Off to Avoid Threatened Lynching
CHANDLER. Aug. 4. — Kid Henderson, who murdered a farmer at Wellston last week, was captured in the northwestern part of the state Saturday, brought back to Chandler, pleaded guilty in court, sentenced to life imprisonment in the penitentiary and taken to McAlester yesterday. His case was handled quietly and the negro hurried off to the penitentiary to avoid threatened lynching.

ed-walls-1915-08-16.A1:
NEGRO SHOT WHILE RESISTING ARREST
Officer A. L. Brookins shot and killed Ed Walls, a negro desperado. this morning at 1:40 o'clock when the later jumped on his partner, Officer J. A. Ellard, from behind and wrenched his pistol from the officer's hand. The shooting occurred at 111 South Thirty-ninth street.

A complaint had been made to police headquarters by Katie Myers, a negro, who asked the officers to arrest the negro Wall. whom she claimed was trying to kill her. Officers Brookins and Ellard were detailed on the call and when they arrived at the above address placed the negro under arrest. Brookins started for the patrol. As he turned his back the negro jumped at Ellard's throat and grabbed the officer's gun. Wall fired twice at Ellard, one bullet taking effect in the padding of his coat and the other passing between his legs. Brookins turned as the negro was pulling the trigger of the revolver the third time and fired on Wall. The bullet took effect in the abdomen and proved fatal.

MISSOURI AND ARKANSAS ARE INUNDATED BY RISING RIVERS Thousands Rendered Homeless Many Drowned Traffic Paralized and Loss will Amout to Millions
(By Associated Press.)

ST. LOUIS, Aug. 23.—The water stood from two to four feet deep in the streets of Valley Park today as the result of the flooding of the Merama river Saturday and Sunday, which drove twenty-five hundred people to the tree tops with a loss according to the coroner of twelve lives. Three hundred miles of the Ozark county are inundated and cut off from communications.

Thousands of farmers are homeless, railroads, telegraph and telephone communication is paralized while the damage is estimated at five million Motorboats are still rescuing the refugees from tree tops.

(By Associated Press.)

LITTLE ROCK, Aug. 23.—Negroes were forced at the points of shotguns to join the whites in an effort to save the Rock Island levee near Newport where floods of the White River are sweeping over its top. One levee has already broken and the costly caseway along Newport Lake has been destroyed. One family of five is reported drowned and thousands of acres are inundated, steamers are rescuing the residents from the bottoms.
newport-newport-1915-08-24.A3:
ARKANSAS' TURN
TO FIGHT FLOODS
White River Breaks Levee at New- port Refugees Plucked From Trees
White river is coming over the Rock Island levee at Newport and the town will be flooded according to report here today. The $25,000 causeway just completed over Newport Lake has broken.

Hundreds of volunteers this morning are working on the levee and negroes have been forced at the point of shotguns to work on the levee.

Reports were received here last night that a family of five persons had been drowned in the bottoms near New Oil Trough. In Newport all business has been suspended, every store in the city being closed.

Virtually every man and boy in Newport responded to a call last night for volunteers to work on the levee which at that time had not broken, but was caving badly in several places. Negroes were forced to join and about 200 men worked until 4 o'clock this morning in an effort to save the levee. They fought a hope less fight, however, as the levee broke in a half dozen places at 4 o'clock.

The damage to crops in White river bottoms will be enormous, as thousands of acres of the most fertile land in the bottoms is flooded.

The steamers Muskogee and Mary G. Lucas are running day and night rescuing families from the overflowed districts. Many of the dwellers of the lowlands are being taken from trees.

The present stage of the water is higher than for 15 years and the river at points above Newport has exceeded the records by the government for 65 years.
newport-newport-1915-08-24.A6:
VOLUNTEERS WORK ON ARKANSAS LEVEES
LITTLE ROCK, ARK., Aug. 23.—The flood waters of White River, which have inundated 100 square miles of land in Independence County, flowed over the Rock Island levee at Newport today.

All business in the town has been suspended.

Hundreds of volunteers are working on the levee and negroes, it is said, have been forced to join them. The Stevens-Steel levee at Ingleside near Newport has broken.

Damage to crops in White River bottoms will be enormous, as thousands of acres of the most fertile land is flooded.

Steamers are running day and night rescuing families from the overflowed districts. Hundreds of heads of stock driven out of the bottoms are roaming the streets of Newport and vicinity.
newport-newport-1915-08-24.A8:
Six Lives Lost By Overflow Of White River
Little Rock, Ark., Aug. 23. Newport, Ark., on the White river, is fighting a flood that threatens to inundate the entire city, according to telegraphic advices to Little Rock today. All business has been suspended and the entire population and farmers for miles around are working desperately to repair six distinct breaks in the levee, according to dispatches reaching here. The reports said white citizens were standing guard with shotguns, compelling negro farm hands to keep at work, threatening them with death if they relaxed. The $25,000 Newport lake causeway, recently finished, went out this morning and the light and power plants are out of commission. Six lives have been claimed by floods elsewhere in Arkansas it was reported here, five at Oil Trough bottom and one, that of C. S. Jordan, a ferry man, at Heber Springs. The situation is the most serious in many years. The White, Black, Ouachita and Buffalo rivers are out of their banks for miles, flooding thousands of farm acres. Batesville is cut off from communication and it is feared a disaster may have occurred there. The state convict farm is flooded. Train schedules have been abandoned in many sections. Damage is roughly estimated at $1,000,000.

The White river levee is broken in six places here. The $25,000 causeway completed over Newport lake went out Monday. The river is coming over the Rock Island levee, and there is no doubt that the entire town will be flooded within a short time.

With the main levee broken in a half dozen places and water rushing over it in many places, the entire city of Newport is threatened with being flooded by the rise in White river. Hundreds of adults, volunteers are working on the levee and negroes have been forced at the point of shotguns to work on the levee.

The Stevens-Steel level at Ingleside, near Newport has broken and the Village creek and White river levee gave way. Judge M. M. Stuckey of Newport is at the head of a gang of forty men who worked in an effort to prevent further damage to the levee.

Reports were received that a family of five persons had been drowned in the bottoms near Oil Trough. Parties from Newport who had been searching the flooded district for refugees said they had been told that a family of five persons, whose names could not be learned, had called for aid, but other refugees were unable to get to them. It is believed that the entire family perished.

In Newport all business has been suspended, every store in the city being closed. The water and electric light plants have been put out of commission by the waters which have already flooded part of the city.

One of the shots lodged in the flesh of the man's right leg. The negro fled but the city police were notified and he was arrested shortly afterward.

Holdup at Willsburg

Mrs. Murphy who was held up near Dillsburg, had returned from market in this city. She was met by her son in an automobile. After going a short distance the highwayman jumped from the bushes and covered them with a revolver demanding their money. After this was handed over he disappeared in the bushes ordering Mrs. Murphy and her son to go on.

Mrs. Murphy said she recognized her assailant as Stewart Chilson, who was a neighbor of her's for several years. She has sworn out a warrant for his arrest. Chilson is said to have figured in a number of sensational criminal offenses in the neighborhood.

ode-johnson-1915-08.A7:
Quarantine Problem
in Criminal Courts;
Now on Argument List
Whether it is illegal to remove all foodstuffs or only food for cattle from quarantined farms, and whether milk from cattle may be considered under the former heading, will be threshed out in argument sessions before the Dauphin County Courts as a result of the termination yesterday afternoon of the trial of Harvey S. Bomberger, a Derry township farmer, for violating the State quarantine act. State Livestock Sanitary Board officials had prosecuted Bomberger and he was on trial in September quarter sessions yesterday when the legal dispute arose and the case was continued until argument court. Bomberger, it was contended, sold milk from his farm while his cattle were under quarantine for the foot and mouth disease. The question of foods and under what classification they should be considered so far as milk is concerned developed and after an hour or more of wrangling the case was taken out of the jury's hands.

Ode Johnson, the negro convicted of assaulting a negro maid and who was arrested following an exciting chase led by Captain George F. Lumb, assistant superintendent of State police, got six months. Other cases disposed of yesterday included: Paul Briggman, guilty, chicken stealing; C. O. Irvine, three charges of false pretense, nine months each; Wilby Ferree and Winfield S. Fisk, burglary, seventy days each in jail. John Carnathan was acquitted of receiving stolen goods. He bought a box of cheap cigars for 10 cents from a youth who is believed to have stolen them. Carnathan had no attorney because he said he "hadn't the money to retain one, but that if the court would give him one he'd pay the attorney as soon as he could earn the money." The court appointed Attorney W. L. Loeser for the purpose and the latter easily had Carnathan acquitted.

sam-johnson-arbuckle-1915-08-03.A1:
Lynch Talk is Heard.
[United Press Leased Wire Service.] ARBUCKLES, Calif., Aug. 3.—Lynch talk was heard among posses today seeking Sam Johnson, who shot Richard Lindsay when the boy protected his aunt, Mrs. Michael Blevins, from the negro. Lindsay dies in a San Francisco hospital today. The shooting occurred on a lonely ranch near near Williams. Sheriffs from from three counties are searching for Johnson.
sam-johnson-arbuckle-1915-08-03.A3:
SEARCH FOR NEGRO
[ASSOCIATED PRESS DISPATCH]

ARBUCKLE, Cal., Aug. 2.—The sheriffs of Colusa. Glenn and Yolo counties, assisted by large posses and bloodhounds, are scouring the foothills west of here in an effort to find Sam Johnson, alleged on Sunday night to have wounded and probably fatally Richard Lindsay when the latter endevored to protect his aunt, Mrs. Mike Blevins, the bride of a wealthy sheep man, from the negro. The shooting occurred on a lonely ranch, and the woman finally drove off the negro. There is talk of a lynching if Johnson is caught.

Johnson was discharged by a negro for whom he had been chopping wood, and learning that Blevins was not at home, started for the sheepman's home. Mrs. Blevins kept him away until her nephew arrived.

The negro shot Lindsay in the arm and breast with a shotgun. This gave the woman time to obtain a rifle. The negro fled and Mrs. Blevins fired, but did not hit him.
sam-johnson-arbuckle-1915-08-03.A7:
California Mob
May Hang Negro
Woodland, Cal., Aug. 3.—Sam Johnson, the negro fiend who attacked Mrs. Michael Blevins at the home in Colusa county and who murdered the woman's nephew, Richard Lindsay, when the boy responded to Mrs. Blevins' cry for help, was captured this afternoon at Capay, ten miles west of Woodland.

When word was received here that the train on which Johnson was being taken to Colusa would pass through here a great crowd rushed to the depot, prepared to mob the negro if they got a chance. The train, however did not stop and officers proceeded to take Johnson to Colusa. Feeling is high at Colusa and violence is feared when the negro is taken from the train.

Jack Woods a young farmer who was a member of the mob searching for the negro, made the capture. Woods saw the fugitive along a creek near Capay and fired at him four times in an effort to cripple him. None of the shots took effect.

The negro exhausted, put up his hands and surrendered. Sheriff Stanton of Colusa county with his posse came up at this moment and rushed away with the prisoner.
The gang of ranchers made threats of lynching but but the sheriff quieted them. The negro pleaded piteously with the sheriff to give him protection.
sam-johnson-arbuckle-1915-08-03.A10:
Negro Murderer Is In Marysville Jail
Sacramento, Cal., Aug. 4.—Sam Johnson, negro who attacked Mrs. Michoel Blevins and murdered her nephew, Richard Lindsay, is in the Yuba county jail at Marysville today. Sheriff Stanton, of Colusa county, negro, fearing to take his prisoner to Colusa yesterday afternoon because a mob had gathered with Blevens, husband of the woman, as ring leader, secured an automobile at Woodland and made a hurried run with his prisoner to Marysville.

Johnson will be kept at the Marysville jail for several days until the excitement dies down and then will be taken secretly to Colusa and placed in the county jail there.

sam-johnson-arbuckle-1915-08-03.A15:
SAM ROBERTSON MUST HANG.
Colusa, Cal., Sept. 4.—Sam Robertson, negro, who killed Richard Lindsey previous to making an attack on Mrs. Michael Blevins, on the Blevins ranca, August 1, was today sentenced to be hanged. Robertson pleaded guilty a few days ago. Today the court heard the testimony of Mrs. Blevins and passed the death sentence.

wellston-wellston-1915-08-07.A1:
NEGRO CHURCH IS DYNAMITED
Wellton Startled by Night Explosion Coming As Aftermath of Lynching at Shawnee
WELLSTON, Aug. 9.—Coming as an echo of the lynching of the negro ravisher Ed Berry at Shawnee, Friday, unknown persons Saturday night exploded a stick of dynamite under the negro church at this place. The explosion aroused the town and damaged the building to considerable extent, tearing off some siding and splintering a section of the floor about twelve feet square. As yet no clue as to the identity of the dynamiter has been secured. Throughout this region there is considerable race feeling as the result of Ed Berry's confessions and his lynching at the hands of a mob.
